nameStory: The Two-toothed Marsh Snail gets its name from the two small tooth-like projections inside its shell opening that help identify it. It's also called the "coffee bean snail" because of its dark brown, oval shape that looks remarkably like a roasted coffee bean you might find in your kitchen.
description: This is a tiny air-breathing snail about the size of a coffee bean that lives in salt marshes along New England's coast. Unlike typical water snails, it can breathe air and actually drowns if kept underwater too long - it's amphibious, splitting time between land and water. The shell is smooth, dark brown to black, and has an oval shape that's taller than it is wide. Most individuals are only about half an inch tall, making them easy to overlook among marsh debris.

idTips.label: Two internal teeth
idTips.description: Look inside the shell opening for two small, white tooth-like projections that give this snail its name - they feel smooth and hard if you gently probe with a grass blade

idTips.label: Coffee bean shape
idTips.description: The shell is distinctly oval and taller than wide, with a glossy brown to black surface that looks and feels smooth like a polished stone

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically about half an inch tall - roughly the size of your pinky fingernail or a large coffee bean

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: The surface feels smooth and slightly slippery when wet, with a subtle shine that catches light like polished wood

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Uniformly dark brown to black with no stripes or patterns - occasionally lighter brown specimens have a coffee-with-cream appearance

idTips.label: Shell opening
idTips.description: The opening is narrow and elongated rather than round, with thick white or cream-colored edges that feel slightly raised

habitat: Look for these snails in salt marshes and tidal areas along New England's coast, especially among the roots of salt marsh grasses like cordgrass. They prefer the upper edges of marshes where they can climb vegetation during high tides but still access the muddy substrate. You'll often find them clinging to marsh grass stems or hiding under debris at the high tide line.

seasonality.spring: Snails become more active as temperatures warm, often seen climbing grass stems during high tides. This is a good time to spot them as they emerge from winter hiding spots.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most visible and easiest to find. Look for them during low tides when they're foraging on mud surfaces or resting on vegetation.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek shelter for winter. They may cluster in protected areas under debris or deep in grass roots.
seasonality.winter: Least active season - they retreat deep into marsh substrate and are rarely visible. Best to search for empty shells washed up by winter storms.

funFact: These snails are actually more closely related to land snails than water snails, and they'll literally drown if kept underwater - they climb up marsh grasses during high tide to breathe air, then slide back down to feed on the mud when the tide goes out!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with small periwinkles, but periwinkles have round shell openings without internal teeth and can survive underwater indefinitely. Remember: if it has two teeth inside and drowns underwater, it's a marsh snail - if it lives happily submerged, it's probably a periwinkle.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - despite being called a "marsh snail," this species breathes air like a land snail and is technically a "pulmonate" (lung-bearing) gastropod rather than a true aquatic snail with gills.
compareHints: The Two-toothed Marsh Snail is the only Melampus species commonly found in New England waters. When comparing to other hollow-shelled snails in the same family, look for the distinctive two teeth inside the shell opening - most related species either have no teeth, different numbers of teeth, or are found in different habitats entirely. The coffee bean shape and amphibious lifestyle also set it apart from its marine relatives.
